dryRun.title: How many calls does fib(n) make? Without memo vs with memo
dryRun.note: Without memo the calls grow by about 1.6× every step (that is O(2ⁿ)). With memo they grow by 2 per step (O(n)), because each fib(k) is computed only once.

think.q:
let calls = 0
function fib(n) {
  calls++
  return n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
}
console.log(fib(5), calls)
why: fib(5) is 5, but it needed 15 calls. The same small values, like fib(2), are worked out again and again.
Draw the call tree and you will see the repeated branches.

think.q:
let calls = 0
const memo = new Map()
function fib(n) {
  calls++
  if (n < 2) return n
  if (memo.has(n)) return memo.get(n)
  const v = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
  memo.set(n, v)
  return v
}
console.log(fib(5), calls)
why: The memo remembers each answer. Calls drop from 15 to 9, and the gap grows fast as n grows.
Calls with a memo follow 2n - 1, so the time is O(n).

think.q:
let a = 0, b = 1
for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  ;[a, b] = [b, a + b]
}
console.log(a)
why: Each round moves the pair one step forward: (0,1), (1,1), (1,2), (2,3)... After 10 rounds a is fib(10) = 55.
This version needs only two variables, so its space is O(1).

think.q: What is the time of the plain recursive fib(n) with no memo?
why: Every call makes two more calls, and the depth is about n. That is roughly 2ⁿ calls.
fib(50) would take hours this way, while the loop does it in 50 steps.

think.q: What is the real problem with the plain recursive Fibonacci?
opts: It solves the same smaller problems again and again (overlapping subproblems)
why: The answer to fib(k) never changes, so computing it twice is pure waste. Remember it once, and reuse it.
This is memoization. It is the first step towards dynamic programming.

try.task: Write fib(n). Return the n-th Fibonacci number: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, then each number is the sum of the two before it. It must be fast for n up to 70.
try.hint: Use a loop with two variables, or a recursion with a memo (a Map or an array). Do not use the plain double recursion.

checks.verify: assert(fib(0) === 0 && fib(1) === 1 && fib(2) === 1 && fib(3) === 2, "check fib(0) to fib(3)")
assert(fib(10) === 55, "expected 55")
const t0 = Date.now(); for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) fib(70); assert(Date.now() - t0 < 200, "too slow, did you use the plain double recursion?")

takeaway.key: Plain recursive Fibonacci repeats work and takes O(2ⁿ). Remember each answer once (memo) or build up from the bottom: O(n), and O(1) space with two variables.
mistakes: Using the double recursion for large n.
Forgetting the two base cases (0 and 1).
Storing the memo but never reading it before computing.
Going past n = 78, where JavaScript numbers lose exact precision.

dryRun.title: Merge the sorted halves [1, 4, 7] and [2, 3, 9]
dryRun.note: Merging two sorted lists needs only one look at each front item, so it is O(n). Merge sort = split in half, sort each half, merge.

think.q:
function merge(a, b) {
  const out = []
  let i = 0, j = 0
  while (i < a.length && j < b.length) {
    out.push(a[i] <= b[j] ? a[i++] : b[j++])
  }
  return out.concat(a.slice(i), b.slice(j))
}
console.log(merge([1, 4, 7], [2, 3, 9]).join(","))
why: Each round takes the smaller front item. When one list runs out, concat(a.slice(i), b.slice(j)) adds the rest of the other.
The merge only works because both inputs are already sorted.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
const mid = Math.floor(a.length / 2)
console.log(a.slice(0, mid).length, a.slice(mid).length)
why: Math.floor(5 / 2) is 2, so the left half has 2 items and the right half has 3.
The halves need not be equal. They only need to be smaller, so the recursion ends.

think.q:
console.log(Math.log2(1024))

How many times can 1,024 items be halved before single items remain?
why: 2¹⁰ = 1024, so there are 10 levels. Each level merges n items in total, so the cost is n × 10.
That is the O(n log n) of merge sort.

think.q: While merging, two items are equal. To keep the sort stable, which one do you take first?
opts: The one from the right half
The one from the left half
why: The left half came first in the original array, so equal items from the left must stay first. That is why the test is a[i] <= b[j] and not <.
Stable sorts matter when you sort objects by one field after another.

think.q: What does merge sort cost, compared with quick sort?
opts: O(n log n) in every case, but O(n) extra space
O(n²) in the worst case, in place
why: The split is always even, so the time is always O(n log n). The merge step needs a helper array of size n.
Quick sort is in place but has an O(n²) worst case. Merge sort trades space for a guarantee.

try.task: Write mergeSort(nums). Return a new array sorted in increasing order using merge sort. The input must stay unchanged. Do not use sort.
try.hint: If the length is 0 or 1, return a copy. Otherwise split at mid, sort both halves with the same function, and merge them with two indexes.

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(mergeSort([5, 2, 4, 1, 3])) === "[1,2,3,4,5]", "expected [1,2,3,4,5]")
assert(JSON.stringify(mergeSort([2, -1, 2, 0, -1])) === "[-1,-1,0,2,2]", "expected [-1,-1,0,2,2]")
assert(JSON.stringify(mergeSort([])) === "[]" && JSON.stringify(mergeSort([7])) === "[7]", "edge cases")
const x = [3, 1, 2]; mergeSort(x); assert(JSON.stringify(x) === "[3,1,2]", "the input was changed")

const orig = Array.prototype.sort; Array.prototype.sort = function () { throw new Error("do not use sort") }; try { const big = Array.from({ length: 50000 }, (_, i) => (i * 7919) % 50021); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = mergeSort(big); let ok = true; for (let k = 1; k < r.length; k++) if (r[k - 1] > r[k]) ok = false; assert(ok && r.length === 50000 && Date.now() - t0 < 1500, "not sorted or too slow") } finally { Array.prototype.sort = orig }

takeaway.key: Split in half, sort each half, merge in O(n). Always O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space, and stable if you take the left item on ties.
mistakes: Forgetting the base case (length 0 or 1) and recursing forever.
Forgetting to copy the leftover items after one half runs out.
Using < instead of <= in the merge and losing stability.
Calling merge on unsorted halves.

dryRun.title: Count the nodes of the tree 1 (2 (4, 5), 3) by recursion
dryRun.note: A tree is a node plus two smaller trees. So a recursive function asks the left and right children, then combines their answers. A missing child (null) is the base case.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
console.log(root.left.right.val, root.right.left)
why: root.left is the node 2, its right child is 5. The node 3 has no left child, so that field is null.
A missing child is stored as null here, not left out.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
function count(n) {
  if (!n) return 0
  return 1 + count(n.left) + count(n.right)
}
console.log(count(root))
why: The tree has five nodes: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Each call adds 1 for itself and asks both children.
if (!n) return 0 is the base case. Without it, null.left would crash.

think.q:
const t = { val: 1, left: null, right: null }
try {
  console.log(t.left.val)
} catch (e) {
  console.log(e.constructor.name)
}
why: Reading .val of null throws a TypeError. Always check that a node exists before you use it.
Most tree bugs in interviews are a missing null check.

think.q: A binary tree has 4 levels (the root is level 1). What is the largest number of nodes it can have?
why: Level k holds at most 2^(k-1) nodes: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15.
So a tree with n nodes can be as short as about log₂(n) levels, or as tall as n (a straight line).

think.q: A recursive function visits every node of a tree with n nodes and height h. What is its extra space?
why: At any moment the stack holds one call per level on the path from the root to the current node: that is h calls.
For a balanced tree h is about log n. For a tree that is a straight line, h is n.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }, and a missing child is null. Write countLeaves(root). Return how many leaf nodes there are (nodes with no children). An empty tree (null) has 0 leaves.
try.hint: Base cases: null gives 0, and a node with no children gives 1. Otherwise add the leaves of the left and right subtrees.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(countLeaves(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))) === 3, "expected 3")
assert(countLeaves(null) === 0, "expected 0")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(countLeaves(T(9)) === 1, "expected 1")

checks.t: a node with only one child
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(countLeaves(T(1, T(2, T(3)), null)) === 1, "expected 1, the node 1 is not a leaf")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(countLeaves(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3, T(6), T(7)))) === 4, "expected 4")

takeaway.key: A binary tree is a node with two smaller trees (left and right). Recursion fits it perfectly: handle null, then combine the answers of both children. Time O(n), space O(height).
mistakes: Not checking for null before reading .left or .val.
Counting a node with one child as a leaf.
Mixing up the tree (nodes) with an array that stores it.
Forgetting that the height of a skewed tree is n, so recursion can overflow.

dryRun.title: The three depth-first orders of the tree 4 (2 (1, 3), 6 (5, 7))
dryRun.note: The three differ only in when the node itself is visited. Inorder on a binary search tree gives the values sorted.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const out = []
function inorder(n) {
  if (!n) return
  inorder(n.left)
  out.push(n.val)
  inorder(n.right)
}
inorder(root)
console.log(out.join(","))
why: Inorder goes all the way left first (4), then 2, then 5, then the root 1, then 3.
Remember: the node is visited in the middle, between its left and right subtrees.

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const out = []
function post(n) {
  if (!n) return
  post(n.left)
  post(n.right)
  out.push(n.val)
}
post(root)
console.log(out.join(","))
why: Postorder visits the node last. Children always come before their parent, so the root 1 is the final value.
This is the order to use when a parent needs its children's answers first (height, size, delete).

think.q: You want to copy a tree. You must create a parent before you attach its children. Which order fits?
why: Preorder handles the node first, then its children, so the parent exists when the children are attached.
It is also how a tree is saved to text, so it can be rebuilt later.

think.q: A binary search tree holds 1 to 7. Which traversal prints 1 2 3 4 5 6 7?
why: In a BST every left value is smaller and every right value is larger. Inorder visits left, node, right, so the values come out sorted.
This is the standard way to check or print a BST.

think.q: What are the time and extra space of a recursive DFS on a tree with n nodes and height h?
why: Every node is visited exactly once, so time is O(n). The call stack holds at most h calls at a time.
In a tree that is a straight line, h = n, so the stack can overflow for very large inputs.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write inorder(root). Return an array of the values in inorder (left, node, right). For an empty tree return [].
try.hint: Use a helper that returns when the node is null; otherwise it visits the left child, pushes node.val, then visits the right child.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorder(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3)))) === "[4,2,5,1,3]", "expected [4,2,5,1,3]")

checks.t: a search tree gives sorted values
checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorder(T(4, T(2, T(1), T(3)), T(6, T(5), T(7))))) === "[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]", "expected 1 to 7")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorder(null)) === "[]" && JSON.stringify(inorder(T(8))) === "[8]", "edge cases")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorder(T(3, T(2, T(1)), null))) === "[1,2,3]", "expected [1,2,3]")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(inorder(T(1, null, T(2, null, T(3))))) === "[1,2,3]", "expected [1,2,3]")

takeaway.key: DFS goes deep first. Preorder = node first (copy), inorder = node between (sorted on a BST), postorder = node last (children first). O(n) time, O(h) stack.
mistakes: Mixing up the three orders (look at where the node is handled).
Forgetting the null base case.
Pushing into one shared array by mistake across several calls.
Assuming inorder is sorted for any tree (only for a BST).

dryRun.title: Level order of the tree 1 (2 (4, 5), 3)
dryRun.note: Read the level size first, then take exactly that many nodes. The new children go to the back of the queue and wait for the next level. Result: [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5]].

think.q:
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r })
const root = T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3))
const levels = []
let queue = [root]
while (queue.length) {
  const size = queue.length
  const level = []
  for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    const n = queue.shift()
    level.push(n.val)
    if (n.left) queue.push(n.left)
    if (n.right) queue.push(n.right)
  }
  levels.push(level)
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(levels))
why: Each pass of the while loop handles one full level. Level 1 is just the root, level 2 is its two children, level 3 is their children.
Without the size snapshot you would get one flat list and lose the levels.

think.q: Why do we store const size = queue.length before the inner for loop?
opts: Because the queue grows while we add children, and we need to stop at the end of the current level
why: Inside the loop we push children, so queue.length keeps changing. The snapshot says how many nodes belong to this level.
This one line is the whole trick for "level by level" problems.

think.q: Breadth-first search needs a ______, depth-first search needs a ______ (or recursion).
why: A queue serves the oldest item first, so nodes are handled level by level. A stack serves the newest first, so you go deep before you go wide.
Swap the structure and you swap the traversal.

think.q: What is the time, and the extra space, of level order on a tree with n nodes?
why: Each node enters and leaves the queue once: O(n). The queue holds at most one full level, so the space is the widest level, up to about n / 2.
DFS uses space by height, BFS by width. Pick by tree shape.

think.q: You need the minimum depth (the nearest leaf). Why is BFS a good choice?
opts: It uses less memory than DFS in all cases
It reaches the nearest nodes first, so it can stop at the first leaf it sees
It visits nodes in sorted order
It does not need a queue
why: Level by level means the first leaf found is the closest one. DFS may explore a very deep branch before it finds a shallow leaf.
The same idea gives the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

try.task: Nodes look like { val, left, right }. Write levelOrder(root). Return an array of levels from top to bottom, each level as an array of values from left to right. For an empty tree return [].
try.hint: Start with queue = [root]. In each round read size = queue.length, take that many nodes, collect their values, and push their children.

checks.verify: const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(levelOrder(T(1, T(2, T(4), T(5)), T(3)))) === "[[1],[2,3],[4,5]]", "expected [[1],[2,3],[4,5]]")
assert(JSON.stringify(levelOrder(null)) === "[]", "expected []")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(levelOrder(T(7))) === "[[7]]", "expected [[7]]")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(levelOrder(T(1, T(2, T(3)), null))) === "[[1],[2],[3]]", "expected [[1],[2],[3]]")
const T = (v, l = null, r = null) => ({ val: v, left: l, right: r }); assert(JSON.stringify(levelOrder(T(3, T(9), T(20, T(15), T(7))))) === "[[3],[9,20],[15,7]]", "expected [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]")

takeaway.key: BFS uses a queue and goes level by level. Take the level size first, then handle exactly that many nodes. O(n) time, O(width) space. It reaches the nearest nodes first.
mistakes: Not snapshotting the level size, so the levels get mixed.
Pushing a null child into the queue.
Forgetting the empty-tree case.
Using a stack by mistake, which turns it into DFS.

flags: Tree questions build the tree with a tiny helper T(val, left, right). Each try-it check repeats this helper so the copyable test script stays self-contained.
fibonacci: the try-it timing check calls fib(70) 2,000 times, which a double recursion cannot pass.
merge-sort: the try-it check temporarily replaces Array.prototype.sort and restores it in finally.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (dry runs of concept lessons are not machine-run). The call counts in the fibonacci table were computed with a script.
